design_detail: Anonymous, unpaid, one-sitting online survey (Qualtrics; designed to take about 50 minutes) from the Johns Hopkins Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research, August 2020 to January 2021, of adults who said they had had changes in their beliefs that they attribute to a psychedelic experience. Respondents chose the single experience 'that you feel led to the greatest belief change' and, at the time of the survey, rated their agreement (-3 to +3) with ten statements about which entities can have conscious experience (self, other humans, non-human primates, four-legged animals, insects, fungi, plants, inanimate natural objects, inanimate man-made objects, the universe), five superstition or paranormal items and one free-will item, each for three time points: 'Before (e.g., a month)', 'After (e.g., a month)' and 'Now'; plus the MEQ30 for the remembered experience and ratings of challenge, personal meaning and insight. 1,606 analysed. Paired t-tests and McNemar tests, with differences counted as meaningful only if p < 1e-5 and d of at least 0.2 (means) or a difference of at least 10 percentage points (proportions); low vs high MEQ (median split); a linear mixed model with MEQ as a continuous predictor and listed covariates. All three time points, including 'before', were rated in one sitting a mean of 8.2 years after the experience (Materials and methods, pp. 2-3). Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as for the same group's similar surveys in the card set.
can_establish: What this self-selected group of 1,606 people, recruited because they attributed a belief change to a psychedelic experience, reported about their beliefs before, after and now, as percentages agreeing with each statement, and that those who rated the remembered experience as more mystical reported larger changes.
cannot_establish: That psychedelic experiences increase the attribution of consciousness (entry required a belief change attributed to a psychedelic, respondents described their most belief-changing experience, and 'before' beliefs were recalled years later, so the before-after difference may reflect selection and recall rather than change); how common such changes are among people who use psychedelics; whether the changes endure (the 'after' and 'now' ratings were made in the same sitting); or whether the beliefs are true, which the authors say the data neither support nor undermine (p. 6).

sample.recruitment: Internet postings on social media and relevant websites (for example Erowid) and email invitations to an anonymous survey for people who had taken a psychedelic that led to changes in their beliefs; the belief changes were intentionally described vaguely, inviting anyone who had had changes in beliefs that they attribute to a psychedelic experience (Materials and methods › Participant Recruitment, p. 2). No compensation (p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or over; able to read, write and speak fluent English; endorsing a belief-changing psychedelic experience with one of the listed classic psychedelics. After consent, sequential exclusions: no English fluency 170; no belief-changing psychedelic experience 264; failed one or more attention checks 38; a drug other than psilocybin mushrooms, LSD, ayahuasca, N,N-DMT, 5-MeO-DMT or mescaline-containing cacti 76; multiple psychoactive drugs 633; age at the reference experience younger than age at first psychedelic use 11; did not complete 2,086; responses appearing to refer to several experiences 113 (Results › Survey Completion, pp. 3-4).
sample.demographics: Mean age 35.1 (SD 13.3); male 67%; White 89%, Hispanic 11%; United States 69%; bachelor's degree 32%, master's 17%, advanced professional degree 8%. Age at the reference experience 26.9 (SD 10.1); years since it 8.2 (SD 12.6); 25% within the past 12 months; for 44% it was their first belief-changing psychedelic experience; lifetime classic psychedelic uses 20.9 (SD 25.7). Substance at the reference experience: psilocybin mushrooms 49%, LSD 33%, ayahuasca 7%, N,N-DMT 6%, 5-MeO-DMT 3%, mescaline 2% (Table 1, p. 4).
sample.attrition: Of 11,281 who reached the landing page, 4,997 consented; 2,086 of those did not complete and 1,305 were excluded for the other reasons listed, leaving 1,606 (editors' arithmetic: 4,997 - 3,391). Non-completers were not compared with completers.
sample.selection_effects: Selection on the outcome: only people who attributed a belief change to a psychedelic were invited, and each described the experience that changed their beliefs most. Recruitment ran through psychedelic-interest websites and social media; people who had combined drugs (633) were excluded. The high rates of agreement 'after' therefore describe a group chosen for having changed, not people who use psychedelics in general.

exposure.measurement: Self-report of the substance (from a list), an estimated dose, other drugs taken, age at the experience and when it happened (p. 2); the MEQ30 rated retrospectively for the remembered experience (mean 74% of maximum, SD 20; 49% met the a priori criterion for a complete mystical experience) and psychological challenge on an 8-point scale (pp. 2-4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported in the article (an estimated dose was asked, p. 2).
exposure.polysubstance: Respondents who reported using multiple psychoactive drugs (633) were excluded (p. 4); other drug use is not reported.

comparison.controls: None. 'Before' ratings are each respondent's recollection at the time of the survey. The Discussion compares the 61% who agreed after the experience that plants can be conscious with 10% or 18% reported in general-population studies (Arico et al., 2011; Reggia et al., 2015), which used other samples and wording (p. 5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Beliefs before the experience were not measured at the time; prior religious or spiritual commitments, interest in questions of consciousness and expectations are not reported in the article.

outcomes.instruments: Ten statements on the capacity of entities for conscious experience (nine entities in assumed descending likelihood, plus 'The universe is conscious'); three superstition items and two items judged a priori improbable (abominable snowman, Loch Ness monster) from the Revised Paranormal Belief Scale; one free-will item; each rated from strongly disagree (-3) to strongly agree (+3) for 'Before', 'After' and 'Now' (Materials and methods, pp. 2-3; Tables 2-3, pp. 5-6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study-made items without validation beyond internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha 0.87 at all three time points for the consciousness items, p. 4); no norms; 'before' ratings are retrospective.
outcomes.operationalization: Agreement = a rating of +1 to +3. A meaningful change = p < 1e-5 and Cohen's d of at least 0.2 for mean ratings, or p < 1e-5 and a difference of at least 10 percentage points for proportions (McNemar tests) (Statistical Analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs, p. 3).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: No formal correction, but very strict thresholds (p < 1e-5 together with a minimum effect size or 10-point difference) for every comparison (p. 3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages agreeing, Before to After to Now (Table 2, p. 5): self 80, 97, 98; other humans 78, 94, 95; non-human primates 63, 83, 85; four-legged animals 59, 79, 82; insects 33, 57, 60; fungi 21, 56, 62; plants 26, 61, 64; inanimate natural objects (for example rocks) 8, 26, 29; inanimate man-made objects (for example chairs) 3, 15, 17; the universe is conscious 34, 80, 82. Every Before-After difference met the criteria (McNemar p < 1e-10 to < 1e-100); no After-Now difference did. Superstitions and free will (Table 3, p. 6): black cats 8, 4, 3; broken mirror 10, 5, 4; number 13 7, 3, 2; abominable snowman 6, 8, 8; Loch Ness monster 10, 10, 10; free will 74, 74, 73; no meaningful changes. Cohen's d values for the mean ratings are in Supplementary Table 2, not among the files (not extracted). Respondents with MEQ at or above the median reported higher 'after' ratings than those below it for every entity except other humans (Figure 2, p. 6); the mixed model with MEQ as a continuous variable is reported only in Supplementary Table 3 (not read).
analysis.covariates: Mixed model: age, age at the experience, sex, race, whether it was the first psychedelic experience, whether it occurred in the past year, number of lifetime psychedelic uses, which psychedelic was taken, and rated psychological challenge (nine variables listed in the Methods, p. 3; the Results speak of eight, p. 5).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned. The data reported are a portion of a larger survey dataset to be reported separately (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Effect sizes and the mixed-model results are only in supplements (not read); the analyses by past-year and first experience are 'data not shown' (p. 4), as is the effect of MEQ on superstition and free-will ratings (p. 5); the sizes of the low- and high-MEQ groups are not given; the rest of the survey is to be reported elsewhere.
analysis.power: No power calculation; the sample is very large relative to the differences tested.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 1,606 people recruited because they attributed a belief change to a psychedelic experience, and describing their most belief-changing one, the shares who agreed that various entities can be conscious were higher for 'after' than for their recalled 'before', all rated in one sitting on average 8 years later: plants 26% to 61%, fungi 21% to 56%, insects 33% to 57%, rocks 8% to 26%, the universe 34% to 80%. 'Now' ratings were similar to 'after'. Superstition and free-will ratings did not change meaningfully (the three superstition items roughly halved from low levels). A more mystical remembered experience went with larger reported change.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title says only that the experience is associated with increased attribution, which fits the design, but the abstract reports large increases, and the Discussion says the survey 'suggests that a single psychedelic experience can increase' these beliefs, that the increases occur soon after the experience and are 'enduring, being unchanged a mean of 8 years after the experience' (p. 5), and that the study demonstrates that attribution increases among people reporting belief-changing experiences (p. 6). Gaps: (1) all three time points were rated at once, years later, so 'soon after' and 'enduring' are recollections, not measurements; (2) recruiting on belief change and asking about the most belief-changing experience build the before-after difference into the sample; (3) a fifth of respondents recalled not agreeing before the experience that they themselves were capable of conscious experience (80% 'before'), which raises the question of how reliably earlier beliefs and the items were answered; (4) the comparison with 10-18% in the general population sets an 'after' figure from a selected sample against other surveys with other wording. The authors acknowledge the retrospective design, the restriction to people reporting belief change and possible demand effects, and call for prospective studies controlling for expectancy (pp. 6-7); their argument that unchanged free-will ratings show the findings are not just demand effects is indirect.

timeline.event: Griffiths et al.: the same group's retrospective online survey of 'God encounter' experiences, whose single-reference-experience method this survey follows (p. 2).
Davis et al.: the same group's retrospective survey of DMT entity encounters, using the same method (p. 2).

Timmermann et al.: prospective online cohort of psychedelic ceremony attendees; agreement with panpsychism and other non-physicalist statements was higher at 4 weeks and 6 months than a week before, among the 122 who answered both follow-ups; cited by this paper (pp. 2, 6).

replication.where_it_stands: The direction agrees with the one prospective study read for this card (Timmermann et al., 2021: a panpsychism item and related beliefs), which however lost about 85% of its baseline sample and had no comparison group. No prospective study that measured beliefs about which entities are conscious before a psychedelic experience, with a comparison group, has been read. The status is partial for that reason.

funding.declared_conflicts: RRG is on the board of directors of the Heffter Research Institute; the remaining author declares no commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest (Conflict of Interest, p. 8).
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors at the Johns Hopkins Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research (R.R. Griffiths also Department of Neuroscience). The funders are private donors and a foundation named in the Funding statement. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that records beliefs about which entities are conscious before a planned psychedelic experience and again weeks and years later, in people not selected for having changed and in a comparison group who do not take a psychedelic, with dropouts followed; or a randomized trial with these beliefs as a pre-specified outcome and expectations measured beforehand.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No frame: internet postings and email invitations.
Self-selected; eligibility required a belief change attributed to a psychedelic, which selects on the outcome.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Demographics and substances are detailed (Table 1), but the setting, amount and context of the experiences are not reported in the article.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Exclusions are documented step by step, but the 2,086 consenting non-completers (42% of those who consented) were not compared with completers.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Study-made items; 'before' beliefs recalled years later in the same sitting as 'after' and 'now'; the MEQ30 answered about a remembered experience on average 8 years old.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: The same online items for all, with alpha 0.87; no test-retest reliability; retrospective framing.
Strict thresholds and an adjusted model, but effect sizes and model results only in supplements not read, a median split, group sizes not given, and error bars labelled as SDs that cannot be SDs.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: No denominator of people reached; 11,281 page visits, 4,997 consents, 1,606 analysed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist (editors' summary: high risk of bias) because the encyclopedia will use the shares of respondents agreeing with each statement. The shares are precise but describe a self-selected group recruited for having changed its beliefs, reporting on its most belief-changing experience, with 'before' recalled years later. Cite for what these respondents reported, with the denominator and the selection stated (for example plants: 26% recalled agreeing before, 61% after), for the absence of change in superstition and free-will ratings, and for the association between remembered mystical intensity and reported change. Not for how often psychedelics change such beliefs, not as evidence that they cause the change, not for durability, and not for whether the beliefs are true.

key_findings.finding: Recruitment and flow: an anonymous online survey for people who attributed changes in their beliefs to a psychedelic experience, recruited through social media, websites such as Erowid and email, August 2020 to January 2021; 11,281 reached the landing page, 4,997 consented and 1,606 were analysed after exclusions (including 2,086 who did not complete and 633 who had used several drugs at the experience).
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Participant Recruitment, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Results › Survey Completion, 1st paragraph (p. 3, continuing on p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Respondents (n = 1,606): mean age 35.1, 67% male, 89% White, 69% from the United States; the reference experience was on average 8.2 years (SD 12.6) before the survey, within the past 12 months for 25%, and the first belief-changing psychedelic experience for 44%; psilocybin mushrooms 49%, LSD 33%, ayahuasca 7%, N,N-DMT 6%, 5-MeO-DMT 3%, mescaline 2%.

About 70% rated the experience among the five most personally meaningful and psychologically insightful of their lives; remembered MEQ30 scores averaged 74% of maximum (SD 20), and 49% met the a priori criterion for a complete mystical experience.
key_findings.locator: Results › Qualities of the Psychedelic Experience, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The 70% figure rests on Supplementary Table 1, which is not among the files.

key_findings.finding: Percentages agreeing that each entity can have conscious experience, Before to After to Now: self 80, 97, 98; other humans 78, 94, 95; non-human primates 63, 83, 85; four-legged animals 59, 79, 82; insects 33, 57, 60; fungi 21, 56, 62; plants 26, 61, 64; inanimate natural objects 8, 26, 29; inanimate man-made objects 3, 15, 17; the universe is conscious 34, 80, 82. All Before-After differences met the criteria (p < 1e-10 or smaller and at least 10 points); no After-Now difference did.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 and footnote; Results › Changes in Attribution of Consciousness, 1st paragraph (p. 4)
key_findings.note: All three columns were rated in one sitting. Figure 1 (p. 5) shows the mean ratings rising, for example plants from about -0.4 to about +0.8, fungi from about -0.3 to about +0.9 and insects from about 0 to about +0.8 on the -3 to +3 scale (read approximately by the editors from a 300-dpi crop).

key_findings.finding: The rise in attribution was reported to be unaffected by whether the experience occurred in the past year or was the respondent's first psychedelic experience (data not shown).
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in Attribution of Consciousness, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Respondents with MEQ scores at or above the median reported larger increases than those below it; 'before' ratings were similar in the two groups, and at 'after' the groups differed meaningfully for every entity except other humans. The relationship held with MEQ as a continuous variable after adjustment for demographic, psychedelic-use and other variables including psychological challenge.
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in Attribution of Consciousness, 2nd paragraph (p. 5); Figure 2 and legend (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Group sizes are not given; the adjusted model is in Supplementary Table 3 (not read).

key_findings.finding: Superstitious beliefs and free will did not change meaningfully: black cats bring bad luck 8%, 4%, 3%; broken mirror 10%, 5%, 4%; 13 is unlucky 7%, 3%, 2%; the abominable snowman exists 6%, 8%, 8%; the Loch Ness monster exists 10%, 10%, 10%; people have free will 74%, 74%, 73% (Before, After, Now).
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in Superstitious Beliefs and Freewill, 1st paragraph (p. 5); Table 3 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: The authors compare the 61% who agreed after the experience that plants can be conscious with 10% or 18% reported in the general population by other studies (Arico et al., 2011; Reggia et al., 2015).

Authors' limitations: a retrospective design, a sample limited to people who endorsed a belief change they attributed to a psychedelic experience, and possible demand effects; they argue that unchanged free-will beliefs suggest the findings are not just an artefact of demand, and state that persistent beliefs after compelling experiences neither support nor undermine the epistemic validity of the beliefs.
The authors call for future prospective psychedelic drug administration studies that control for expectancies.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 6, continuing on p. 7); Abstract, Discussion

reporting_issues.issue: Figures 1 and 2 say the data are means plus or minus 1 SD, but the error bars span only about 0.07 scale points either side of the mean on a -3 to +3 scale (read from a 300-dpi crop of Figure 1), far too short for SDs of ratings on which, for example, 20% did not agree; their length fits standard errors or 95% confidence intervals of the mean in a sample of 1,606 (editors' reading).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures understate the spread of individual ratings; they should not be read as showing that respondents answered alike.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the income band 125,000-199,000 is printed as 0%, between bands of 10% and 9%, and the income rows sum to 89% (editors' arithmetic); the other categorical blocks with complete categories (marital status, education, substance) sum to 100%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a misprint (about 11% may belong in that band); income composition cannot be relied on.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods list nine covariates for the mixed model (age, age at the experience, sex, race, first experience, past-year experience, lifetime uses, substance, psychological challenge), while the Results say the model controlled for eight variables.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; which model was run cannot be confirmed without the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the increased attributions did not decrease in those who completed the survey years after the experience, but the main text reports only that the effects did not depend on whether the experience was in the past year, with data not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: The durability claim rests on an analysis that cannot be checked from the article, and on retrospective 'now' ratings.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor wording differences: the agreement category +1 is 'Somewhat agree' in the Methods and 'Slightly agree' in the table footnotes; the figure axes are labelled from -2 (Disagree), although the rating scale runs from -3.
